content: 1. For children aged 6–17 years, while direct outcome estimations for this population were not available, extrapolation was considered reasonable. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded that an all-oral regimen containing bedaquiline could be used in eligible children within this age group, provided that specific considerations for companion drugs in the regimen, particularly bedaquiline, are taken into account. 2. For pregnant and lactating women, additional evidence is required to better inform the use of the all-oral, bedaquiline-containing shorter regimen (BDQ-LFX/MFX-ETO-E-Z-Hh-CFZ). Ethionamide, a component of this regimen, is generally contraindicated during pregnancy. Omitting or replacing this drug could significantly compromise the regimen's effectiveness. Therefore, for pregnant and lactating women, an individualized, all-oral longer regimen that includes bedaquiline is recommended. 3. In cases of extrapulmonary tuberculosis (TB), due to the lack of evidence on disease severity or extent, clinical judgment is advised when deciding on the use of this regimen for patients with extensive TB disease or severe forms of extrapulmonary TB. 4. The interest in reducing the duration of treatment for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) has led to studies exploring shorter regimens under both programmatic and trial conditions. Eligible patients now have the option of a shorter, injectable-sparing regimen lasting 9–12 months. Proper patient selection is critical to ensure the regimen's effectiveness, prevent the development of additional drug resistance, and protect the regimen components. 5. Routine drug-susceptibility testing (DST) for rifampicin and fluoroquinolones must be guaranteed in settings where the shorter regimen is implemented. Additionally, efforts should be made to expand access to DST for all relevant drugs and to develop and roll out DST methods for newer medications. 6. Monitoring for resistance to other anti-TB drugs should follow WHO recommendations. In the absence of specific DST for bedaquiline, resistance should be monitored through minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) assessments. 7. The use of linezolid in treatment regimens has shown favorable outcomes when combined with bedaquiline in longer regimens. However, until new evidence becomes available, the GDG does not recommend including linezolid in the shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen. Countries are encouraged to consider modified regimens containing both bedaquiline and linezolid only under operational research conditions. 8. A patient-centered approach is essential to support full adherence to treatment. This includes providing necessary patient support and ensuring active monitoring and management of adverse events through functional TB drug safety monitoring systems. 9. Research priorities include studies comparing all-oral shorter regimens containing both bedaquiline and linezolid, assessing their effectiveness and safety in different subgroups, including pregnant and lactating women. Additional research is needed to explore mechanisms of resistance acquisition to bedaquiline, identify genetic markers for resistance, and standardize data collection to contribute to global recommendations. 10. MDR/RR-TB remains a significant global public health threat, with only 30% of estimated cases receiving treatment in 2018. Despite improvements in diagnostics and medications, global treatment success rates remain low, emphasizing the need for continued advancements in treatment strategies. 11. Observational data suggest that the all-oral bedaquiline-containing shorter regimen of 9–12 months is as effective as longer regimens containing bedaquiline. The shorter regimen offers advantages such as reduced loss to follow-up and better tolerability without significant toxicity. 12. The GDG judged the overall certainty of evidence for the shorter regimen to be very low due to reliance on observational data and potential residual confounding. While programmatic data reflect real-world practice, their applicability to other settings may vary based on factors such as HIV prevalence, drug-resistance patterns, and quality of healthcare services. 13. Stakeholder perspectives, including those of patients and civil society representatives, highlight preferences for treatment regimens with minimal disruption to normal life, fewer side effects, and shorter durations. Injectable agents and severe side effects were deemed unacceptable by most participants. 14. The balance of effects between desirable and undesirable outcomes favors the use of the all-oral shorter regimen in appropriate settings, provided that patient selection and monitoring are carefully managed.
